conceptTitle.text: Proposal · Hard board as a live circuit board

conceptNote.text:
Design proposal for the Hard board (shown on Level 2, OR, already built). Flip A and B to watch it work.

• A real PCB look: dark green board, gold solder pads on every pin, silkscreen labels, orthogonal copper traces instead of curves.
• Visible power: an IN +5V terminal block feeds an always-live amber rail. Transistors only work when a C leg is wired to it (no hidden power).
• Current you can see: lit traces carry moving dashes in the direction of flow; dark traces are dull copper. Motion stops when the phone asks for reduced motion.
• Transistors use the classic circle symbol (base bar inside, collector to the rail, emitter arrow to the bus), like the Normal workbench; slide switches; an LED with a glow.
• A tool bar (Place / Wire / Probe / Erase) makes each tap's meaning explicit. Probe would show a pin's value.
• A logic analyzer replaces the truth-table tiles: A, B, want and OUT as waveforms across the 4 steps.
• The header shows OUT live.

startTitle.text: App start · Continue or New game → difficulty

startNote.text:
The app opens here (before the Journey map). One save slot, on the phone.

CONTINUE: shown only when a game exists. The card shows the current level, progress, the game's difficulty and the Hard ★ count. Tweak 'hasSave' to see first launch (New game only).

NEW GAME → choose Normal or Hard. This sets the game's default: each lesson's main button starts in that mode ('Start · Hard'), and the other mode stays one tap away ('Play this level in Normal'). Levels without a Hard version yet play in Normal. Starting over an existing save asks first: 'Erase your progress?'.

level6Title.text: Level 6 — half adder · lesson and Hard mode

l6Hard.text:
Level 6 Normal is artboard 6 in the top row (sockets; its back button now goes to this lesson).

HARD: no sockets and no hint about which chips. The palette has one of each gate (AND, OR, NAND, XOR) and two fixed LEDs, C (carry) and S (sum). Place two chips, wire A and B into both, then each chip to its LED. Run test reads both LEDs per row (want 00 / 01 / 01 / 10). Shown solved: AND → C, XOR → S. A switch wired straight to an LED is rejected.

level2Title.text: Level 2 — OR gate · Normal and Hard mode

sharedBench.text:
Two modes per level, chosen on the lesson screen. Either one completes the level; Hard adds a ★ on the Journey map.

NORMAL: one shared workbench (goal → board → wiring row → A / B / Output → want/got truth table). Level 1 fixes Stacked; Level 2 lets you choose.

HARD: the Sandbox editor with a goal. A, B and OUT are fixed; the palette holds only this level's parts (Transistor ×2). Place, wire, then Run test plays all 4 rows. Rules so shortcuts can't pass: switches drive only a transistor's base, and the LED must be driven by a transistor. Shown here already solved; tap A and B.

flowTitle.text: Bit by Bit — learn a computer from the transistor up

srNote.text: Level 15 opens Memory. New idea: feedback. Two NOR gates, each output looped into the other gate (the amber 'loop' buttons). Starts with one NOR placed and one loop connected. Set/Reset are short pulses (on for about half a second, then off), so the player sees Q stay put after the input goes away. New tool: a timeline (S, R, Q) instead of a truth table, since memory depends on order, not just inputs. The test plays a fixed pulse sequence and draws wanted vs actual Q, with mismatches in red. S + R shows the forbidden state; letting both go at once shows a race (Q flickers).

calcNote.text: Milestone payoff: a working 8-bit calculator (0–255, + and −) made only of the player's own chips. Use it: a real 7-segment display; the line under it shows the bus in binary and the code of the last key. X-ray: the same calculator as a chain of the chips built in Levels 10–13, with live values. Latch A is a dashed Chapter 4 preview (holding a number needs memory), which sets up the next chapter. Three sums to finish: 125 + 99 (carries), 42 − 100 (negative, no Cout), 200 + 100 (shows OF overflow).

subNote.text: Level 9 teaches two's complement: the 4-bit ADD chip is now one fixed block. A − B = A + (every bit of B flipped) + 1. Put NOT on all four B lines and set Cin to 1. Starts as 7 − 5 with one NOT placed and Cin = 0. Forget Cin and the test hints 'off by one?'. The ± Signed switch re-reads every number with the top bit worth −8, introducing negative numbers. XOR also works (its 2nd pin is tied to 1), hinting at the ALU's add/subtract switch.

a4Note.text: Level 8 is the first level about real numbers: bits are laid out right to left like written addition, with decimal shown on top. The puzzle: fill 4 sockets with FA chips and connect the 3 carry links (the amber arrow buttons). Starts as 5 + 3 with bits 0–1 built and the bit 1→2 carry missing; once every socket is filled, a wrong sum turns red. Test all 256 checks every sum and names one that fails. HA in bit 0 also passes (bonus line).

faNote.text: Level 7 reuses the HA chip just unlocked: two half adders plus a gate that joins the two carries. New tool: Run all 8 tests the whole truth table at once (8 rows is too many to flip by hand). OR or XOR both work in the carry socket, since both carries are never 1 together; XOR earns a bonus line. Starts with one HA placed.

haNote.text: Level 6 works at chip level, not transistors: pick chips from your toolbox, drop them in the Sum and Carry sockets, then test all 4 rows. A wrong chip shows red rows. Starts with XOR placed and Carry empty.

howItWorks.text:
Core loop: Map → Lesson → Workbench → Level complete → the new chip lands in the Toolbox and becomes a single block for the next level.

The map shows a mid-game save (current level: Half adder). Lesson, Workbench and Complete show Level 1 (AND from two transistors) as the example.

ladder.text:
Abstraction ladder (24 levels):
1 Logic gates: AND, OR, NOT, NAND/NOR, XOR
2 Arithmetic: half adder, full adder, 4-bit adder, subtractor
3 Calculator (milestone)
4 Memory: latches, flip-flops, registers, RAM
5 Mini computer (milestone): PC, decoder, control, run a program

mapTitle.text: Proposal · Game-style level map in 3D (dark board vs bright island)

mapNote.text:
Design proposal: the Journey map as a game level-select. Tap any chip; change 'current' to see other save points.

• The map is a real circuit board tilted in 3D (CSS 3D: perspective + rotateX). Each level is a chip that stands on it with a top, front and side walls, gold pins and a shadow.
• Done chips are green and raised, the current chip is the tallest, amber, and gently bobs with a glow under it. Locked chips sit low and gray with just their number.
• The path is a copper trace. Played sections are lit with current flowing along them; the way ahead is a dashed dark trace.
• Chapters are zones of the board (silkscreen labels). Each chapter ends in a large milestone chip (here the Calculator ★).
• Signs stand upright above chips: earned stars over done levels, the level name over the current one.
• The header keeps the goal in view: 'Your computer · N of 24 parts' and the star total. The card below shows the tapped level: Play, Replay, or 'Finish Level N first'.
• Stars per level (proposal): solved, fewest chips, no hints. Motion stops when the phone asks for reduced motion.

mapBrightNote.text:
Bright variant, in the style of a casual 3D mobile game (Unity-style). Same map, same logic; tap any chip, change 'current' to see other save points.

• A sky with drifting clouds; the board is a floating mint island with thick rounded walls and a soft shadow underneath.
• Toy-like chips with soft light: done = glossy green with gold stars above, current = big orange block that bobs, with a white PLAY tag and sparkles, locked = pale gray with the level number. The milestone is a purple BOSS block.
• The played path is a fat yellow trace with white current running along it; the way ahead is a dotted white line.
• A chunky HUD: star counter and difficulty as white pills; progress as a CPU badge with a fill bar.
• The panel below uses big game buttons with a pressed-down bottom edge (Play, Replay, 'Finish Level N first').
• Rounded display font (Fredoka) for headings and numbers; this would replace Space Grotesk on the map if chosen.

This goes against the current dark 'breadboard' design rule, so it is a choice: bright map only, or a bright theme for the whole app.
